title: Quoting both sides
objectives: Set a two-sided quote around a fair value.
Compute expected profit per minute from the half-spread and the arrival rate

screens.prose: You traded spread against volume. Each side trades $\lambda(s)$ times a minute and earns $s$ a share each time: $$\pi(s) = 2s\,\lambda(s) = 2s\lambda_0 e^{-ks}$$ Here $\lambda_0 = 10$ trades a minute and $k = 0.5$ per penny.
screens.question: What does the factor 2 in $\pi(s)$ count?

options.text: The two sides: buyers at the ask and sellers at the bid
The full spread, $2s$, earned on every trade
options.why: You charged each trade the whole spread. One trade earns $s$ against fair value; it takes two trades to keep $2s$.
The rate of trades is $\lambda(s)$, not 2. The 2 is there because there are two sides.

hints.text: Where did the 2 come from when you worked out the profit at 3p?

feedback.correct: Two sides, each trading $\lambda(s)$ times a minute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about the doubling you did at 3p.

explain.text: Buyers lift your ask and sellers hit your bid, each at rate $\lambda(s)$. Each trade earns $s$, so the two sides give $2s\lambda(s)$.

screens.prose: Now find the best half-spread for any $\lambda_0$ and $k$, by setting the slope of $\pi(s)$ to zero.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\pi(s) = 2\lambda_0\, s\, e^{-ks}$: two sides, each earning $s$ on $\lambda_0 e^{-ks}$ trades a minute
$\pi'(s) = 2\lambda_0 e^{-ks} - 2k\lambda_0\, s\, e^{-ks}$: the product rule on $s \cdot e^{-ks}$
$\pi'(s) = 2\lambda_0 e^{-ks}(1 - ks)$: take out the common factor
$e^{-ks} > 0$, so $\pi'(s) = 0$ only when $1 - ks = 0$, that is $s^* = 1/k$
$\pi'(s) > 0$ below $1/k$ and $\pi'(s) < 0$ above it, so $s^*$ is the peak

hints.text: Start from the profit formula, then differentiate it.
Differentiating $s\,e^{-ks}$ needs the product rule.
Formula, derivative, factorise, set to zero, then check it is a peak and put in $k$.

feedback.correct: The slope is zero only at $s = 1/k$, and it changes from up to down there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the formula, differentiate, factorise, then solve.

byKey.l2: The derivative needs the formula above it first.
byKey.l4: Setting the slope to zero is easiest once it is factorised.

explain.text: The factor $1 - ks$ carries the sign of the slope: positive below $1/k$, negative above. So profit rises to $s^* = 1/k$ and falls after it. A market where traders flee faster (bigger $k$) needs a tighter quote.

widget.solution:
from math import exp

def expected_profit(s, lam0, k):
    """Expected profit a minute, in pence, for one-share trades.
    s: half-spread in pence
    lam0: trades a minute on each side when s = 0
    k: how fast trading falls as s widens, per penny
    """
    rate = lam0 * exp(-k * s)  # trades a minute on each side
    return 2 * s * rate

byKey.no-shares: You kept 1p per round trip. Each round trip is 1,000 shares, so it keeps £10.00.
byKey.pence: That is the answer in pence. Divide by 100 for pounds.

explain.text: $10{,}000 \times 1{,}000 \times 1\text{p} = 10{,}000{,}000\text{p}$, which is £100,000. That is before exchange fees, technology and staff. Two lessons on we meet a bigger cost: losing to traders who know more.

ideas: A market maker bids at $V - s$ and offers at $V + s$; a round trip keeps the whole spread $2s$.
Each single trade earns only $s$, and wider quotes trade less, so profit per minute is $2s\lambda(s)$.
With $\lambda(s) = \lambda_0 e^{-ks}$ profit peaks inside, at $s^* = 1/k$; at $s = 0$ it is zero.
